1.	That the period for the payment of the annual grant to the commission, at present fixed at sixteen years from the first day of April, 1927, be extended to thirty years from the first day of April, 1928, the said annual payment to remain at the sum of $250,000;

That the commission may issue securities and the governor in council may authorize the guarantee of the payment of principal and interest thereon, the proceeds to be deposited to the credit of the Minister of Finance in trust for the commission and released by the minister in his discretion for the purposes of the act;

That a sinking fund shall be created and maintained by the commission out of its actual annual income to provide sufficient funds to redeem such guaranteed securities as they respectively become due, and the provisions of the Expropriation Act instead of the railway act shall be made applicable to proceedings of the commission.

ANGLO-EGYPTIAN TREATY On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext: Has the Prime Minister any statement to make to the house with regard to the relationship between this country and Great Britain in respect to the treaty between Great Britain and Egypt?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon. friend had not asked the question which he has just asked, I was about to request the house to allow me to make a statement on a matter of public interest which -arises out of a report that

Anglo-Egyptian Treaty
appears in to-day's papers to the effect that Lord Salisbury, leader in the House of Lords, of the British government, apparently entertained a different point of view with respect to Canada having been asked to become a party to the Anglo-Egypt.ian treaty from that which was expressed by myself in this house in the course of a debate earlier in the week. May I first of all draw the attention of the house to what Lord Salisbury himself observed, namely, that he had not seen my remarks at the time at which he was speaking and therefore he was unaible to say exactly what had been said by myself in that connection? May I also add that I have not seen the despatches that have gone from Canada to Great Britain and I am therefore not in a position to know what has been represented in Great Britain with respect to the remarks which I made in this house? My remarks however are in Hansard, and with respect to what appears in the Hansard report of the debate of the other night I have nothing to alter or change in any particular. I think I can indicate very clearly where any difference in point of view that may exist has arisen, if such in fact is the case.
Lord Salisbury's remarks, as reported in the papers of yesterday and to-day, fall really under four heads. In the first part Lord Salisbury refers to the policy of Great Britain with respect to the Anglo-Egyptian treaty and remarks that it was a policy for the preservation of peace, and that in that particular the policy of the home government is the same as that of the Canadian government. There is no disagreement in any way between us on that; in fact, we are in hearty accord.
Lord Salisbury then refers to the report which was sent of my remarks on the Chanak incident. I ^hiuk I had better read what Lord Salisbury says in that regard and I can then indicate whether or not there is any difference in our point of view with respect to that jncident. Lord Salisbury's remarks as reported in the Canadian Press cable despatch appearing in the different papers, are as follows:
Undoubtedly, Lord Salisbury continued, relations between the component parts of the empire in respect to these high matters were a matter of some difficulty. Undoubtedly the Canadian government were asked to associate themselves with the British government at the time of the Chanak affair, and were asked whether they would be represented by a military contingent in the event of military action being required in those regions.
It was true, Lord Salisbury declared, there were no military operations, but he would not like to lay it down that the result was entirely 5610^-*ia
due to the action of the Canadian government. His recollection was that there was a very strong feeling in Great Britain against military operations on that occasion, and it would not be rash to say that the strong opinions expressed here had at any rate a partial effect, just as the opinion of Canada had, in bringing that incident to the end it reached.
That is entirely the view I took with respect to the effect of Canada's representations on the Chanak appeal, if I might use that expression. I believe it was one of the factors which operated. I have never contended that it was more than that. I agree absolutely with Lord Salisbury in what he says as to the different factors that materially contributed to bring about the termination of the incident to which reference is there made.
The third part of Lord Salisbury's remarks is as follows:
The government leader continued that in regard to the Anglo-Egyptian treaty it was difficult to discuss the matter because he had not yet received the full text of Premier King's observations. He emphasized that all through the negotiations leading to the draft treaty with Egypt the dominion governments had been kept fully informed of every step taken, but the terms which the British government proposed to the Egyptian government were expressly limited to the relations between that government and Great Britain, and on the face of it did not include any of the dominion governments.
My hon. friend who has asked me a question to-day asked me a question in the house on March 9 last with respect to the Anglo-Egyptian treaty. Here is what was then saic; as it appears in Hansard of that date:
Mr. J. S. Woodsworth (Winnipeg North Centre): I should like to ask the government if Canada has been consulted with regard to the policy of Great Britain in Egypt.
Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King (Prime Minister): I assume that my hon. friend refers to a treaty which was in the course of negotiation between Great Britain and Egypt?
Mr. Woodsworth:	Yes.
Mr. Mackenzie King: The treaty to which my hon. friend has reference was a treaty being negotiated between His Majesty, as representing Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and Egypt. The Canadian government was kept informed of the progress of the negotiations.
So that thus far there is no conflict in anjr particular between the statements made by Lord Salisbury and those made by myself. I did state as long ago as March the 9th last that the treaty negotiated was between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and Egypt, and that we had been kept informed of the policy of the British government with respect thereto. Let me now continue with the further remarks of Lord Salisbury:
There never was any question of asking the dominions to participate in responsibility for the results of the treaty, he said. The dominions were asked to concur in the general

Anglo-Egyptian Treaty
Perhaps my right hon. friend could conveniently now give the date of the first draft treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The despatch that I am referring to was received on November the 11th of last year, 1927.
The report of the inter-imperial relations committee of the Imperial conference, 1926, provides that:
Til the case of a treaty applying to only one Part of the empire, it should be stated to be made by the king on behalf of that part.
To the despatch of November 11 we replied on November 22, stating that the Canadian government would raise no objection to His Majesty's government in Great Britain entering into an agreement embodying the substance of the draft treaty, in appropriate form, with the government of Egypt; however, that we could not contemplate recommending to parliament that the treaty should be made applicable to Canada, nor could we undertake to participate in its signature and ratification, and we gave our reasons therefor.
On November 24 we received a despatch, saying that the British government was much obliged for the full explanation given of the position of the Canadian government in relation to the proposed treaty with Egypt.
On December 2 we received a further despatch, saying that the British government had decided to sign the proposed treaty, in view of the replies received from the various dominions; that it was being made clear that, as regards the form, the treaty should be concluded in the manner contemplated in the report of the inter-imperial relations committee of the Imperial conference, 1926, in case of a treaty made on behalf of one part of the empire, that is, that in the preamble it should be confined to Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and should be signed by a plenipotentiary holding a full power limited correspondingly.
Is that the Prime Minister's deduction, or is it stated in the despatch?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I am giving the substance of the despatches. Hon. members will observe that I am careful to say nothing about the treaty itself. The Imperial government has laid on the table of the British House of Commons all the documents that I think it wishes to have made public with respect to the treaty. I am confining my remarks to the exchange of communications between the British government and our own on the subject of Canada's relation to the treaty.
And the final form in which the treaty was executed differed from the original form submitted to the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend has it exactly. May I say to him that the accuracy of what I have stated from the Canadian point of view is conclusively borne out by the white paper which was laid on the table of the House of Commons of Great Britain this year, entitled Papers regarding Negotiations for a Treaty of Alliance with Egypt, a copy of which I hold in my hand. At page 9 of this white paper is the counterdraft approved by His Majesty's government July 28, 1927. The preamble reads:
His Majesty the King of Great Britain, Ireland and the British Dominions beyond the Reas, Emperor of India, and His Majesty the King of Egypt.
Then after another paragraph or two comes the following one relating to the powers:
Have agreed to conclude a treaty for this purpose and have appointed as plenipotentiaries:
After a blank the paragraph continues:
Who, having communicated their full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed as follows:

Then follows the text of the treaty. Now, under the interpretation set forth by the interimperial relations committee on treaties, a treaty, so drafted, without limitation had it been signed by a plenipotentiary, would have bound Canada along with all the other dominions. Being presented with the full text of the treaty in this form, and being asked to give our concurrence, we interpreted that Canada was asked to be a party to the treaty, and therefore in our reply we were careful to state that we could not become a party to the treaty because, for reasons given we did not believe that this parliament would approve of Canada being made a party thereto.
Now, on pages 35 and 36 of the white paper to which I have already referred appears the draft treaty as it was submitted two days after our despatch, or at any rate after our despatch had gone to Great Britain, stating the position of the Canadian government. The draft is in this form:
His Majesty the King of Great Britain, Ireland, and the British Dominions beyond the Seas, Emperor of India, and His Majesty the King of Egypt,-
I am leaving out some of the intervening paragraphs in the preamble.
Have agreed to conclude a treaty for this purpose, and have appointed as plenipotentiaries:
Immigration oj Miners

His Majesty the King of Great Britain, Ireland, and the British Dominions beyond the Seas, Emperor of India: _
for Great Britain and Northern Ireland:
The Right Honourable the Lord Lloyd, G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E., D.S.O.. Member of His Most Honourable Privy Council:
His Majesty the King of Egypt:
His Excellency Abdel Ivhalek Sarwat Pasha, President of the Council of Ministers;
Who, having communicated their full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed as follows:-
Hon. members will notice that the treaty as finally presented, signed between Great Britain and Egypt, is distinctly limited in the preamble, as should be the case when a treaty applies to only one part of the empire, by saying:
His Majesty for Great Britain and Northern Ireland
Making no reference to any other parts of the empire.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I accept unreservedly Lord Salisbury's statement to the House of Lords that the government of Great Britain had not any intention of obliging the dominions to become a party to the treaty, or even of inviting them to do so.

They made a very delicate suggestion.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING' I agree with my hon. friend, I think it was a very delicate suggestion; and I submit that, as presented to us, the documents were not capable of any other interpretation in the light of the rules laid down at the Imperial conference with respect to the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties. But I hope the explanation which I have made will remove any possibility of difference on that point as between the British government and ourselves.
May I ask the Prime Minister: Egypt then is regarded as a foreign country as the treaty is made with it? Secondly, Canada is not involved in the treaty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, Canada is not bound by the treaty.
And Egypt is a foreign country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend will have to consult some international authority on that point.

There is one matter which
I would like again to bring to the attention of the house, arising out of these tariff adjustments and also having relation to the strike which is taking place in Oshawa. I have no desire to interfere in any way with the efforts being made by the Minister of Labour to bring about a settlement of that dispute; I wish him every success, and hope he can help in an amicable adjustment as between the company and the men. However, when a concern such as the General Motors Corporation cuts wages to the extent of 40 per cent, I cannot help but protest in this house against such action. In a recent issue of the Oshawa Times the general manager of that corporation stated that the average wage of the highest paid workers in that plant is approximately $150 per month. Taking the wages on that basis, this 40 per cent cut will reduce them to not more than $100 per month for the highest paid mechanic, and you can understand the effect that will have on the lower paid workers.
May I ask a question? Were these wages cut generally, or were they cut in some certain departments?

The wages have been reduced, in certain departments, but the other men and women employed in that industry feel that if this cut is accepted their wages also will be cut. I am glad that the Finance minister says he will look into this matter. Anyone who has been closely connected with the motor car industry or has been in the agency business knows that soon after the tariff was reduced on the lower priced cars from 35 to 20 per cent there was a reduction in the price of these cars, but whereas the tariff reduction amounted to 15 peir cent, the reduction in the price of the oars amounted to only 10 per cent. I think that reduction was made by the manufacturers for a purpose. Shortly

after the tariff was reduced by 15 per cent the automobile manufacturers came to parliament and promised that if the excise tax were removed they would pass that reduction on to the consumer. To my mind what really happened after the excise tax was removed was that the remaining 5 per cent of the 15 per cent tariff reduction, which would have to go in the course of time in any event, was passed on to the consumer; and the reduction of the excise tax was taken advantage of by the manufacturers themselves and no corresponding reduction was made to the consumer. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move that the following be inserted in the resolutions amending the Special War Revenue Act:
That Part IT of the Special War Revenue Act, chapter 179, revised statutes of Canada, be repealed as from the 31st of December, 1927.
The explanation of this amendment is as follows: Part II of the Special War Revenue Act imposes a tax of 1 per cent upon the gross interest from loans and investments in Canada and upon the gross income from business transacted in Canada. Such tax is a deduction from the tax otherwise payable under the Income War Tax Act. There is but a small collection of revenue under this act over the amount that would otherwise be collected under the Income War Tax Act, and rather than have a multiplicity of taxes this is repealed. Further, the excess apart from Income War Tax that is collected is generally from companies that have no profits, as the tax under the Special War Revenue Act is upon the gross income or interest.
It is estimated that the reduction in revenue will not exceed $30,000. It will save a lot of bookkeeping, and probably the loss in revenue will be more than offset by the gain in respect to administration.

It has been a surprise to me that the law has remained as it is for so long. It was entirely an emergency
tax, the idea of the tax being, of course, to get money at the earliest possible moment and in as large sums as possible. I think the tax was imposed in 1915.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: It was subsequently looked after by the Income Tax Act and income derived from all lines of business carried on in Canada by -those companies was immediately taxable in gross; this one per cent charge was taken from it. When the Income Tax Act came into force it was apparent that it would be absolutely unjust to keep up two sets of taxation; but on the other hand money was exceedingly scarce and the burdens of the country exceedingly great, and accordingly the old act was retained for the purpose of reaching those who otherwise would not be taxable under the Income Tax Act. Well, we have had the exemptions enlarged, and this act should have gone with those exemptions long ago. I have no doubt that what my hon. friend says is absolutely correct, that it is costing just as much in keeping this out-of-date measure upon our statutes as is collected under it.

Mr. ESLIN'G: I should like to say a word, Mr. Chairman, on the very important in-
Copper Bounties Act

dustry to which the resolution refers. It provides for an extension of the bounty of i cent per pound until June 31, 1931, on copper bars and rods manufactured in Canada and sold for consumption in Canada from copper produced in Canada from ore mined in Canada. We have here an indication of some desire to encourage the creation of Canadian payrolls by the production and manufacture of one of our resources. This bounty is available to any individual or syndicate of individuals who choose to invest their capital in the construction of refineries. It is true that at the present time there is but one beneficiary, but I have been advised by well-informed operators that before the period of this extension expires there will be a very decided change, resulting in more and larger refineries being established. To-day, so far as I can learn, outside the United States there are but three copper refineries in the world. One is in Australia, another in Canada and a third in Japan.
You can readily understand what an enormous output the United States has when it is stated that 96 per cent of the world's copper supply is controlled and refined in that country. We have simply five per cent remaining for these other three refineries. The Canadian refinery is located in Trail, in the district of W'est Kootenay, British Columbia. It produces 10,000 tons, or 20,000,000 pounds of refined copper per year, valued at approximately 33,000,000. But in addition to the refined copper turned out at Trail, there. is produced in Canada raw copper, copper matte and blister copper to the value of $12,000,000. This entire output is shipped to the United States, where it is refined. These properties are located largely on the Pacific coast. They are controlled by United States interests, and naturally those interests are quite willing to have the raw material go to the States where wages are expended in refining it.
Not only do we lose the wages paid on refining this raw material in the United States, but out of $12,000,000 worth shipped to that country $7,000,000 worth is returned to Canada for consumption here. As the United States control 95 per cent of the world output, they also control the price, and they take advantage of that control by fixing two prices, one for home consumption and the other for export, the export price being $8 per ton in excess of the domestic price. So that the copper control of the United States enables their operators to say to the world at large: That is our price; you will pay us

$8 a ton in excess of what we sell for home consumption or you may leave it, just as you please.
Now, with the enormous production there you can understand that the United States has the advantage also of refining copper more cheaply. This will be readily apparent when I state that at the refinery in Trail they turn out 20,000,000 pounds per year, while in just one tankroom in the plant at Anaconda, in the States, they turn out 17,000,000 pounds in one month-a very decided difference. We all realize what wonderful activities are in progress in a mining way throughout the Dominion to-day. In fact, I think it is generally admitted that these activities have just started.

Did I understand the
hon. member to say that the refinery at Trail is working at full capacity, or not?

No. I say it refines 10,000
tons or 20,000,000 pounds a year. I say there is so much mining activity to-day that in a very short time there will be more smelters, more concentrators and more refineries in the Dominion, particularly if they are given proper encouragement. The prospects are so bright, I have been informed, that before the period expires for the payment of this bounty there will be refineries in Canada producing 100,000 tons of refined copper per annum. One hundred thousand tons of refined copper produced from ore mined and smelted in Canada would not only create an enormous payroll but would open various avenues of business and trade, and you can readily understand the prosperity that would follow. It would not only create Canadian payrolls but it would go very much farther, by enabling Canada to care for the copper and metal requirements of the British Empire. The empire to-day purchases from $40,000,000 to $50,000,000 worth of copper annually from the United States and on that purchase of forty or fifty millions is paid this excess of $8 per ton on such as is not manufactured. The last figures available of exports from the United States to various parts of the Empire are for 1926, but they are very fair indications of what the 1927 figures will show. In the year 1926 the United States exported copper to the United Kingdom to the value of $29,000,000; to Canada, $6,500,000; to British India, $846,000; to Australia, $214,000; to Hong Kong, $135,000; to British South Africa, $155,000; and the balance to other sections of the empire. You can see, therefore, the absolute hold which the copper trust of the United States has on the empire at large and you can

Copper Bounties Act
readily understand how urgent it is that this condition should be changed, because every country over which the British flag floats pays that excess of $8 per ton. In view of what has happened in the past there is nothing in the world to prevent this copper trust from saying, "We will make it $18 instead of $8 . And Canada would have to pay the toll in common with the rest of the empire. This possibility is emphasized by our experience during the war. When the allies needed copper the United States control simply said, "Our price is 31J cents and it will have to be paid". And it was paid. The hon. leader of the opposition the other day referred to the zinc situation during the war, when the United States controlled the world's zinc supply. They then fixed the price at 44 cents per pound, and it was due entirely to the work of the research laboratory at Trail, which solved the problem of treating zinc ores, that the smelter there was able to break the combine and provide the allies with zinc at from 12 to 15 cents per pound. That result is to be attributed to research. You can go back further in the research work and other activities on the part of the Trail smelter and you have the interesting fact that that smelter perfected the process of refining lead by electricity, as a result of which Trail had the first electrolytic lead refinery in the world. Hon. gentlemen all know that the major portion of our asbestos goes to the United States as well as the greater portion of our nickle, where these products are manufactured and shipped back to us in the finished state in very large quantities. Last year there came back to the empire $1,000,000 worth of asbestos products on which wages were paid in the United States, and there was shipped to the empire at large $1,000,000 worth of Canadian nickel manufactured in the States.
Obviously, therefore, this is a very important subject. When we consider the prospects of our mineral development we can see that the result will be the establishment of smelters, concentrators and refineries, and this will mean not only more Canadian pay cheques for Canadian workmen but, if the government is so disposed, it will mean the protection of the empire's metal requirements against foreign control and price dictation.
As a result of the recent imperial conference Canada, we are told, had assumed a new constitutional status and was now an independent nation. Be that as it may, the fact remains that our geographical status is the same. Our borders are open on three sides and just so long as Canada remains withm the empire we shall be absolutely and directly
dependent upon the mother country for protection. You cannot get away from that. But we are becoming so carelessly indifferent to that fact that we are forgetting that to-day our security rests entirely with the British navy; and for that security and protection we contribute not one dollar to the British exchequer. It sounds well, no doubt, to be referred to as an independent nation, and it adds to our national pride to feel that we are almost a great nation. But it seems to me that it would be everlastingly to the credit of Canada if at the same time we could be stamped in the eyes of the world as a grateful nation; and I think the best way we could show our gratitude would be by protecting the empire's needs for such minerals and metals as we produce. I do not think the government would make any mistake if it formulated a policy whereby the minerals and metals of this Dominion might be conserved for the use of Canada and of the empire at large, so as to render us absolutely free from the dictation and price control of a foreign country. I am quite confident that Great Britain would co-operate and lend encouragement, and very probably other assistance, in carrying out such a policy, and I am equally confident that this house and the country generally would heartily approve of any measure which would free Canada and the empire from the price control and dictation to which it is now subjected.

Coming from British Columbia, I am naturally in favour of the extension of this bounty, which I think was started in 1923. I remember the criticism made against it at that time. It has been well said that the lines of political thought are devious, and I could not help thinking of that when I heard the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) tell us we should support this extension because of our gratitude to the British Empire for the protection afforded us by the British navy. According to the statement of the hon. member Canada produces about five per cent of the copper production of the world; if the United States controls 95 per cent of the production, I do not think the British navy will be materially affected by what we do in connection with a fractional part of that 5 per cent, because we are not granting a bounty on the entire Canadian production. I am not familiar with the conditions at Trail; I have never been there, but I believe it is one of the largest smelters in Canada, and if I am not mistaken it is controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I must suppose that the tons there are different from the tons in other parts of British Columbia, because the hon. member stated that the output was 10,000 tons or 3,000,000 pounds.
No, valued at $3,000,000.

I accept the correction, but
I have another point to bring up. The hon. member has told us that the body which controls the price of copper in the United States has a habit of fixing the price of copper to be used in Canada or any other place outside the United States at $8 a ton more than the United States price. I would suggest that that is a pretty liberal protection in itself for Canadian manufacturers. So to start with, we have a protection of $8 per ton if the statement of the hon. member for West Kootenay is correct, and on top of that we 
have this bonus ranging from one and a half cents to one-half cent per pound, or from $30 to $10 per ton, so it would seem to me that the Smelter Co. is being fairly well taken care of.

Is this the same concern
which controls the smelting of lead at Trail?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, lead and zinc.

There are some interesting facts in that connection. There is a duty of $20 a ton on lead, and some of us were very interested to find the other day that the people who use lead in the manufacture of paint, for example, buy their lead from Trail and pay that duty. This company which furnishes the lead takes full advantage of that duty except for about ten cents per hundred, which just enables them to hold their trade. One interesting feature which we discovered is that the price paid at Montreal for the lead bought from Trail is the price of lead on the London market plus the duty, plus the freight from London to Montreal. The Montreal price has no relation to the freight rate from Trail to Montreal, except when navigation closes on the St. Lawrence and the freight from London to Montreal goes up about 25 cents a hundred because it has to be landed at Halifax. Then, almost automatically, the smelter at Trail raises the price of the lead by exactly that amount, so the whole evidence is that the lead smelter at Trail is taking the full advantage of the duty with the exception of just enough to enable them to hold the trade. Paint is used very extensively in Canada, and it would be used a great deal more if we could get it at a lower price. In view of the conditions which prevail in regard to lead, and I think I have stated them fairly, this kind of bonus or protection to an institution which is taking full advantage of the Canadian consumer does not appeal to us very strongly.

I hope our protectionist
friends will take note of that.

With regard to this bounty on copper it is interesting to remember that just a few years ago the predecessor of the present Minister of Finance discontinued the bounty on crude petroleum because fields were being opened in Canada which would draw very heavily on the treasury of the country if the bounty were continued.
I would point out that the same condition will obtain in the copper industry, because in the very near future the production of copper in this country will amount to something it is hardly possible to imagine, from the oper-

Copper Bounties Act
ations which are now taking place in the northern parts of some of the western provinces. In view of this fact I think it would be well for the minister to consider whether this extension should not be limited to one year, or to two years at the most.
The amount of the bounty would not be affected by the copper production. The bounty is paid on the refined copper, and it takes two or three years to build refineries.

I should like to say just a few words in support of this resolution. It is all very well' to laugh at the small production which we have obtained in Canada so far, but this smelter at Trail is one of the achievements in Canada of which we might well be proud. We only wish we had an equally large smelter in eastern Canada. Some years ago I pointed out the benefits to Canada derived from this smelter. Mention was made here to-day of a mine somewhere near Stewart. If there was a smelter near Stewart, we would be refining a great deal of lead. The Trail smelter only takes care of its own field, and the result is that the ores from such places as Stewart have to be sent to the refineries of the United States.

The statement is made
that ores can be shipped from Stewart by way of the Panama canal to Swansea, Wales, at a cheaper rate than they can be shipped to Trail.

Quite true. There
is a refinery near Stewart which is also American.
I should like to point out that the present production is largely due to the work of the prospector, and if you study conditions in eastern Canada and Northern Ontario and Quebec you will find the situation to be this: For some years prospectors were taught to look for gold and silver, and the result was they found no other minerals. During the last few years, however, they have been taught to search for copper, lead and zinc, and they find these minerals in great quantities in northern Ontario and Quebec. If this bounty is continued-although I am not in favour of a bounty, as of some other form of protection-we will have a smelter established in eastern Canada equal to that at Trail. Then there will be competition and a reduction in price, and in _**-'tern Canada we shall be in a more independent position. There is no question about it. For- years the International Nickel Co. has been operating round
Sudbury but it has confined its work to nickel. We have tremendous fields of copper the result of persons being taught to look for them. They are now being discovered by prospectors trained in our mining schools, and the result is that in a very few years the development will be something beyond what any person in Canada can now imagine.

I concur in the remarks
which have been made by the hon. member for Kingston. Few of us are aware of the tremendous possibilities in connection with the recent discoveries that have been made in northern Ontario and northern Quebec. Our copper industry is in its infancy, though in the district which I have the honour to represent we have been producing copper for forty years. We also supply 85 per cent of the world's nickel. Recently there has been discovered in the nickel fields of Ontario one of the largest copper deposits on the American continent, and one of the strange features of this discovery is that this copper was found in connection with nickel. When the nickel mine at Frood had been sunk to a depth of over 3,000 feet a tremendous body of high grade copper ore was discovered; and to-day the International Nickel Co. and the Mond Nickel Co. have entered into a development that will entail an expenditure of eighteen or twenty million dollars. It would be almost fatal to the copper industry at the present juncture if the present bounty were discontinued. If there was any time in the history of the copper industry when the bonus should be maintained it is now. There has been discovered in one mine alone, the Frood mine of the International Nickel Co., a body of high grade ore which has an estimated value to-day of over $1,000,000,000. This is only one of the mines in the district adj oining these big copper deposits. Discoveries of lead and zinc have also been made and these promise to become sources of tremendous wealth to Canada. There is no doubt that with the continuation of this bounty, you will see in the Sudbury district within a very few years, one of the largest smelters on the American continent. The International Nickel Co. have also laid the foundations for a smelter the estimated cost of which is nearly $10,000,000. They have completed their shaft, 17+ by 20 feet, to a depth of 3,044 feet, and it is the largest on the American .continent. They have localized their ore bodies, and are now in a position to go ahead and develop their mines. Imagine for a moment what the effect would be on this industry if the bounty were discontinued at the present time. Copper is one of the basic metals of
Special War Revenue Act

the world to-day and industry is continually finding new uses for it. Would it not be unwise in view of the great amount of prospecting that has been done, and the large amount of capital which has been invested in the mining industry, to remove the bounty at the present time? There is no doubt in the minds of those who are familiar with the geological formation of our great pre-Cambrian shield that the discovery of copper on this scale is only one of the many discoveries that will be made in the near future, and I am very much in favour of having this bounty continued.

I have just one comment to make and that is with respect to the somewhat singular argument that has been advanced in support of the continuation of this bounty. We have been accustomed to hear that owing to the mass production in the United States they can flood our market with cheap goods, and the Dumping Act has been applied to prevent products from the United States being sold at a lower rate than the rate at which they are sold in the domestic market. Now we are asked to provide a bounty for the copper industry and one of the reasons advanced in its support is that products from the United States are being sold here at a price which is $8 higher than the rate in the domestic market. On the one hand it seems that action must be taken to prevent the importation of articles from the United States at a lower price than is current there, and on the other we are told that we must have this bounty because we are charged an excessive price by United States smelters. I am not in favour of the bounty, although I should like to see Canadian ores refined in Canadian refineries, but some of the arguments that have been advanced are singular, to say the least.

Then I
would like to ask the minister what is the reason for the increase of $68,000.

This is a progressively increasing work, and naturally it requires an increasing amount of money each year, especially the eradication of bovine tuberculosis. As a result of the suspension of the export trade in cattle to Great Britain, we have been able to extend the work much more rapidly this year as we have been able to use the services of twenty-five veterinarians who had been formerly engaged in accompanying shipments of cattle exported overseas, but even with this help we are not able to keep up with the applications from the various provinces for the organization and establishment of further restricted areas for the eradication, so far as is humanly pos-56103-119
sible, of tuberculosis in cattle. It is the extension of that work that is the main reason for this increase.

In view of the large amount involved in this item and the contentious nature of the purpose for which the sum is voted, I think it will be proper for the minister at this stage to make a report to the house covering the operation of the plan to date, and giving the percentage of reduction in bovine tuberculosis wherever eradication has really occurred, as well as the total cost of the scheme if it is to be extended over the immense area of Canada. The minister will perhaps be at greater ease if I concentrate my suggestion to him in a single sentence. What I would like him to do is now to make a report to the committee on the operation, success, and future of the bovine tuberculosis eradication plan.
That is under the restricted area plan. There are three plans.
Cover the whole business.

The restricted area plan was first adopted in Manitoba, at the request of the provincial Department of Agriculture there, in 1923. At first it took in just three municipalities, and the area was extended to four a year or two afterwards. That area was not only the first restricted area in Canada, but the first in the British Empire. About a year after that, a restricted area was established in the province of Quebec in the counties of Bieauhamois, Huntingdon, and Chateauguay. This was extended last year as far as the Richelieu river and was further extended this year from the Richelieu river to the St. Francis river. Next, the whole province of Prince Edward Island was made a restricted area, and we found there the smallest percentage of reactors in any province of the Dominion. Only 0.59 per cent of the total cattle population of the Island reacted to the test, if I remember aright. Then about two and a half years ago, we established an area in the Fraser river valley in British Columbia. That is the source from which New Westminster and Vancouver get all their milk supply.
That statement is true in so far as the initial test is concerned.

Six municipalities
in Last Mountain formed the next restricted area, and that has not been extended, although there are applications in for its en-

Immigration Act

largement. Next, we established a small area in New Brunswick about ten miles out from the city of Fredericton, containing about two or three thousand cattle. A year ago this spring Prince Edward county in Ontario was organized as the first area of this nature in this province. In Nova Scotia we have practically the whole province, in hand, with the exception of Cape Breton island. Twenty-nine veterinarians have been there since last October, and will continue possibly until about July 1. It is considered that Cape Breton is sufficiently segregated from the rest of the province to avoid any risk of contagion being spread to the mainland from there. The farmers of Cape Breton island are not quite ready to ask for this service until they see how it results in the other parts of the province. I think all the information in connection with this matter is contained in very concise form in a return to an inquiry by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland).
